```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("theme.R")
library(housepi)
set.seed(42)
```

Let's briefly recall the concept of Bayesian data augmentation for the case of epidemiological outbreaks.

Bayesian data augmentation is a computational strategy that expands the parameter space by introducing augmented variables to facilitate sampling from the posterior.

Consider a single infectious individual $i$.
Imagine that someone reported the exact time of symptom onset ${t}^{(\mathrm{ons})}_{i}$ .
We can introduce latent infection times ${t}_{i}$, defined as the difference between the onset time and the augmented incubation period ${\tau}^{(\mathrm{inc})}_{i}$:

$${t}_{i} = {t}^{(\mathrm{ons})}_{i} - {\tau}^{(\mathrm{inc})}_{i},$$

where we the incubation period drawn from a model distribution.
Say $y$ the observed data (onset and status), $z$ the augmented variables (infection time and incubation oeriod), and $\theta$ the parameters (for transmission and augmented variable models), the joint posterior reads

$${P}({\theta}, {z}\vert{y}) \varpropto {P}({y}\vert{\theta},{z}) {P}({z}\vert{\theta}){P}({\theta}).$$

This choice preserves the marginal posterior of interest.

For the Monte Carlo Markov Chain Through iterative sampling from these conditional distributions—drawing Z(t+1) \~ p(Z\|Y,θ(t)) followed by θ(t+1) \~ p(θ\|Y,Z(t+1))— the method generates a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the joint posterior p(θ,Z\|Y), and whose θ-marginal converges to the target posterior p(θ\|Y).

We here explain how to associate individual augmented variables in `housepi` for minimal examples.

# Example: estimate incubation periods distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a dataset which is not a household survey.
Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate its parameters augmenting the infection and onset times.
We model both augmented variables as uniformly distributed in the reported ranges.

```{r}
# use an example script for generate delays
source("generate_delays.R")

# generate delays according to a gamma distribution
dataset <- generate_delays() |>
  # correct right censoring to allow the event to occur during the whole day
  # note: temporary before allowing for expaned arguments
  dplyr::mutate(exposure_max = exposure_max + 0.99,
                onset_max = onset_max + 0.99)
head(dataset)
```

# Build augmented variables

Similarly to parameter, augmented variables require definitions for models and proposer rules needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo.
In many applications, augmented variable definitions can also depend on the dataset or on model parameters to be inferred.

We can link an argument value to its source with the character "\@", e.
g.
"onset_max\@D" will link to the value at individual data "onset_max".
More in general, definition arguments `value`, `args`, `min`, `max`, `scale` and `from` can be linked to external values in the following ways

| Origin    |    Link Examples    | Symbol |
|-----------|:-------------------:|:------:|
| Augmented | "proba", "proba\@A" |   A    |
| Dataset   |   "onset_max\@D"    |   D    |
| Parameter |      "mean\@P"      |   P    |
| Scalar    |  14, "14", "14\@S"  |   S    |

The model has the only requirement to associate an augmented variable `"log_proba"` for each individual with positive status.
This variable will be used to compute the log-probability of the incubation period distribution.
We propose the incubation period to be distributed as a gamma distribution, with parameters `shape` and `scale` to be inferred.
Then, we define the augmented variables `infec_time` and `onset_time` as uniformly distributed in the ranges of exposure and onset times, respectively.

```{r}
# generate an instance of the household model class
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("augm example") |>

  # augmented variable definitions as function calls
  load_augmented_list(
    # declare 'incub_period' as the difference
    # between augmented onset and infection times
    incub_period = "onset_time - infec_time",

    # explicit declaration of incubation period distribution
    ..proba = list(
      func = "gamma_meanvar", # gamma distribution (by mean and variance)
      func_args = c(
        x = "incub_period",   # compute from individual augmented 'incub_period'
        mean = "mean@P",      # use model parameter 'mean'
        var = "var@P"         # and 'var'
      ),
      max = 14                # truncation
    ),

    # declare the augmented variable 'log_proba'
    log_proba = "log(..proba)"
  ) |>

  # define the gamma distribution parameter to be inferred
  load_parameter_list(
    mean = list(prior = "unif", args = c(min = 0.1, max = 5), rule = "norm"),
    var = list(prior = "unif", args = c(min = 0.1, max = 5), rule = "norm")
  )

hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  # add 'infec_time' time definition
  add_augmented(
    name = "infec_time",
    value = "exposure_min@D", # start from data value 'exposure_min'
    # uniform model within the range [0, 'exposure_max']
    model = "unif",
    args = c(min = 0, max = "exposure_max@D"),
    rule = "norm", # normal distribution for the mcmc proposer 
    scale = 0.25   # with scale 0.25 (i. e. standard deviation)
  ) |>
  # add 'onset_time' time definition
  add_augmented(
    name = "onset_time", value = "onset_max@D",
    model = "unif", args = c(min = "onset_min@D", max = "onset_max@D"),
    rule = "norm", scale = 0.25
  )
```

# Extract augmented variable draws

We could run the inference and extract the results as usual.
However, sometimes we might be interested in extracting also to check if augmented variables evolve as expected.
We can do so by providing in the setup arguments of `infer()`, the `id` of individual whose augmented variables we want to store.
Notice that we had to introduce an auxiliary augmented function `..proba`.
The name starting with `..` is a convention for housepi to interpet such as private and don't store its draws.

```{r}
#| warning: false
hhmodel |>
  add_dataset(dataset) |>
  infer(n_steps = 10000, n_burnin = 500,
        thin = 8, n_chains = 4, n_adapt = 3000,
        # store augmented draws for individual "7"
        id_draws = "7", 
        progress = FALSE) |>
  get_param_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 2))
```

Note that here the dataset has no demographic structure.
We are assuming all individuals livto live in distinct households.

# Other proposer rules for the augmented variables

```{r}
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

When it comes to data augmentation, we might need to explore different options for the Monte Carlo moves.
In the following examples we show the differences between move choices that can be performed.
As shown in [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html), we do the testing with the "blank" model.
We always recommend a visual assesment before choosing a new move.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 2
#| warning: false
# with model (default sample)
new_housepi_model("blank") |>
  add_augmented(name = "sample from model",
                model = "norm", args = c(mean = 14)) |>
  infer() |> 
  get_augm_draws() |> 
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()

# random walk starting from 0 (without model)
new_housepi_model("blank") |>
  add_augmented(name = "random walk", value = 14, rule = "norm") |>
  infer() |> 
  get_augm_draws() |> 
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()

# independent normal moves from value 87 (without model)
new_housepi_model("blank") |>
  add_augmented(name = "independent moves", rule = "norm", from = 14) |>
  infer() |> 
  get_augm_draws() |> 
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```
